title: Headache at the Three-Month Review
objective: Students recognise a severely raised blood pressure in an older adult, interpret symptom-driven pill-taking, prioritise ineffective health self-management as the nursing diagnosis once signs of an emergency are absent, plan adherence support around the client's own barrier, prevent a duplicate dose, and evaluate the adherence plan.
population: Older adult, 71-year-old man with hypertension and type 2 diabetes
setting: Chronic disease clinic, district health centre, Trinidad
endpoint: Adherence plan agreed, improvement at the one-week review, and home blood pressure monitoring with ongoing clinic follow-up

opening.narrative: Rawle, a 71-year-old man and retired maxi-taxi driver, attends the chronic disease clinic at the district health centre for a scheduled three-month review, accompanied by a daughter. Rawle says, "I have a little headache since I wake up this morning, but is nothing serious." History includes hypertension for 12 years and type 2 diabetes for 6 years. Prescribed medicines are amlodipine 10 mg once daily, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg once daily and metformin 500 mg twice daily, collected free each month from the health centre pharmacy under the Chronic Disease Assistance Programme. No known drug allergies. Rawle lives alone and goes to the market by maxi-taxi three mornings a week; the daughter visits at weekends. Breakfast was at 6:30 am. The district medical officer (DMO) is running the clinic this morning.

stages.narrative: The nurse completes the initial assessment.

assessment.finding: Alert and oriented to person, place and time. Speech clear. Pupils equal and reactive to light. Hand grips equal.
Heart sounds regular. Capillary refill under 2 seconds. Pedal pulses palpable. No ankle oedema.
Breathing even and unlaboured. Chest clear on auscultation.
Abdomen soft, non-tender, bowel sounds present. Appetite usual; bowels open daily.
Moves all limbs freely. Walks steadily without an aid.
Thick callus under the right big toe joint. Skin intact, no redness or drainage.
Rawle says, "The pressure always up when I come here. Is the clinic that does do it."

stages.narrative: After 15 minutes' rest, the nurse repeats the blood pressure: 182/110 mm Hg. Asked how the tablets are taken, Rawle says, "I does take them when I feel the pressure up. This morning when the headache start, I take one of each pressure tablet with my breakfast." The daughter adds, "Daddy say the water tablet have him running to the toilet, so he leave it off when he going to market."

On focused questioning, Rawle denies chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness or numbness of the face or limbs, and any change in vision. The headache is unchanged. The nurse finds Rawle alert, with clear speech, equal hand grips and no facial droop. The DMO will examine Rawle next and has asked for an ECG and a urine dipstick.

The DMO examines Rawle. Fundoscopy shows no haemorrhages and no swelling of the optic discs. The DMO documents no evidence of acute organ damage and records a working diagnosis of severe hypertension without acute organ damage, with the prescribed tablets taken irregularly. Blood results from the last visit, three months ago, are on the record.

The DMO tells Rawle and the daughter that both pressure tablets will continue at the same doses, with a nurse review in one week. The DMO then writes on the treatment sheet: "Amlodipine 10 mg orally, stat, from clinic stock. Recheck blood pressure before the client leaves," and moves on to the next client. The nurse takes the tablet from stock and goes to Rawle.

After speaking with the nurse, the DMO cancels the stat amlodipine because Rawle took the usual morning dose at 6:30 am. The nurse, Rawle and the daughter then agree an adherence plan, and the DMO approves the change in dose timing: the daughter fills a weekly pill organiser every Sunday; both pressure tablets are taken each morning, and on market days the hydrochlorothiazide is taken on returning home, no later than 2 pm; the nurse will telephone midweek. At 11:00 am the blood pressure is 168/102 mm Hg and Rawle reports no new symptoms. Rawle goes home with advice to attend A&E for a severe headache, chest pain, weakness or change in vision, to have blood taken at the health centre on day 5, and to return in one week for review.

medications.name: Amlodipine
medications.status: Cancelled by the DMO 10:15 am; usual dose taken 6:30 am

medications.name: Hydrochlorothiazide
medications.frequency: Once daily, morning; on market days on returning home, no later than 2 pm

stages.narrative: Rawle returns for the one-week review with the daughter, who brings the pill organiser. When the nurse telephoned midweek, Rawle said all was well.

vitals.label: Blood pressure
vitals.value: 144/88 mm Hg (seated, left arm, after 5 minutes' rest)

assessment.finding: Alert and oriented. Reports no headache since the last visit.
Heart sounds regular. Pedal pulses palpable. No ankle oedema.
Breathing even and unlaboured. Chest clear on auscultation.
Abdomen soft, non-tender, bowel sounds present. Appetite usual.
Reports passing more urine in the mornings than before. Not waking at night to pass urine.
Moves all limbs freely. Walks steadily; no dizziness on standing.
Callus under the right big toe joint unchanged. Skin intact.
Every compartment of the pill organiser for the past seven days is empty. The daughter says the Sunday filling "takes five minutes".

medications.name: Hydrochlorothiazide
medications.frequency: Once daily, morning; on market days on returning home, no later than 2 pm

stages.narrative: While updating Rawle's record, the nurse rereads their own notes from the last three clinic visits. Each records a raised blood pressure and "advised to take medication regularly", with nothing about whether doses were being missed or why.

The daughter has bought an automatic upper-arm blood pressure monitor for Rawle to use at home. Rawle says, "Good. Now I could check it when I feel the pressure going up." The next clinic review is booked for four weeks' time.

questions.stem: Which finding should the nurse recognize as requiring immediate follow-up?

options.label: A
options.text: Random blood glucose of 168 mg/dL

options.label: B
options.text: Callus under the right big toe joint

options.label: C
options.text: Blood pressure of 186/112 mm Hg

options.label: D
options.text: Says the clinic visit makes the reading rise

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: A reading of 186/112 mm Hg is at or above 180/110 mm Hg, the severe range, in a 71-year-old who also has diabetes and a headache since waking. A reading this high needs follow-up now: a repeat after rest, a check for signs of acute organ damage (brain, heart, eyes, kidneys) and a report to the DMO. The other findings matter at this visit but carry no immediate risk.

distractor_rationales.A: Rawle has diabetes and ate about two hours ago, so a random glucose of 168 mg/dL is within what is expected after a meal. It belongs in the review of diabetes control, not in immediate follow-up.
distractor_rationales.B: A callus on the foot of a client with diabetes is a real risk for ulceration and needs foot-care teaching or referral at this visit. The skin is intact, so it can wait until the blood pressure has been dealt with.
distractor_rationales.D: The clinic can raise a reading a little, but a client's explanation cannot be assumed to account for 186/112 mm Hg. The reading must be repeated and acted on, not explained away.

questions.self_test: The callus needs attention at this visit, but intact skin is not an immediate threat, whereas a pressure above 180/110 mm Hg with a headache could be.

meta.priority_principle: Act on the finding with immediate risk before chronic-care findings
meta.prerequisites: Blood pressure categories in adults; diabetic foot risk; expected post-meal glucose
meta.suggested_review: Blood pressure measurement and severe-range readings in primary care

questions.stem: How should the nurse interpret the significance of Rawle's account of taking the tablets?

options.label: A
options.text: Doses depend on symptoms, so many days pass untreated

options.label: B
options.text: The diuretic's side effect means it should be stopped

options.label: C
options.text: The morning doses should soon bring the reading down

options.label: D
options.text: The two medicines are no longer strong enough for Rawle

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: Rawle takes the tablets only when the pressure is "felt", and leaves out the hydrochlorothiazide on market days. Hypertension usually causes no symptoms, so on most days nothing tells Rawle to take a dose and the pressure goes untreated. That explains a reading still at 182/110 mm Hg after rest, and it rests on a belief the nurse can work with.

distractor_rationales.B: Passing more urine is an expected effect of hydrochlorothiazide, not a harmful reaction. It is a real barrier, but the answer is better timing of the dose, not stopping a drug that is needed.
distractor_rationales.C: Amlodipine takes hours to reach its peak and about a week of regular doses to give its full effect, and a thiazide also lowers pressure over days to weeks. One catch-up dose at 6:30 am will not control the pressure by mid-morning.
distractor_rationales.D: Drugs cannot be judged to have failed when they are not being taken regularly. Rawle's account points to missed doses, so the regimen has not yet been tested.

questions.self_test: Treatment failure is tempting because the reading is high on two drugs, but Rawle's account shows the drugs are taken only on some days, so they have not had a fair test.

meta.priority_principle: Establish adherence before judging treatment response
meta.prerequisites: Asymptomatic nature of hypertension; onset of amlodipine and thiazides
meta.suggested_review: Assessing medication adherence and its barriers

questions.stem: At this point, which nursing diagnosis should the nurse prioritize for Rawle?

options.label: A
options.text: Risk for ineffective cerebral tissue perfusion related to a blood pressure of 182/110 mm Hg after 15 minutes' rest

options.label: B
options.text: Ineffective health self-management related to belief that pressure is felt and diuretic urgency, as evidenced by skipped doses

options.label: C
options.text: Acute pain related to raised blood pressure, as evidenced by a frontal headache of 3/10 since waking

options.label: D
options.text: Deficient knowledge related to misunderstanding of how blood pressure varies, as evidenced by blaming the clinic for the reading

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: Two problems compete: the severe pressure's risk to the brain, and the way Rawle manages the tablets. Rawle takes them only when the pressure is "felt" and leaves out the hydrochlorothiazide on market days because of the trips to the toilet, and the pressure is still 182/110 mm Hg after rest. That is an actual problem with its evidence on screen, and it is the cause of the severe reading. A risk problem comes first only when it is the more immediately dangerous, and here it is not: focused questioning found no chest pain, breathlessness, weakness, numbness or change in vision, speech and grips are normal, and the headache is mild and unchanged. Without signs of organ injury, severe hypertension is not lowered urgently, because a rapid fall can itself reduce blood flow to the brain; it is brought down over days with regular oral doses. So the nurse's first target is the dose-taking pattern, which is how the perfusion risk is actually reduced.

distractor_rationales.A: A severe reading does put the brain at risk, and this would be the priority if there were confusion, vomiting, visual change, new weakness or a worsening headache. Rawle has none of these, so the risk is not immediately dangerous, and urgent lowering would do harm rather than good. The nurse keeps watching for those signs, but the risk is reduced only by treating the actual problem behind it: the skipped doses.
distractor_rationales.C: The headache is real, but at 3/10 it is mild and is a result of the raised pressure, not the problem itself. Relieving it would not lower the pressure, and focusing on it could reinforce Rawle's belief that the tablets are for when the pressure is felt.
distractor_rationales.D: Rawle's comment that the clinic raises the reading does show a gap in understanding, and teaching will be part of the plan. But Rawle has lived with hypertension for 12 years, and the key evidence is behaviour: doses taken only with symptoms, and the diuretic left off on market days for a practical reason that information alone does not remove. When a knowledge gap is one cause of a wider problem, it belongs in the etiology; ineffective health self-management covers the belief, the practical barrier and the skipped doses that keep the pressure high.

questions.self_test: Risk for ineffective cerebral tissue perfusion is tempting because the pressure is above 180/110 mm Hg, but with no signs of injury to the brain the risk is not immediately dangerous, and it comes from the skipped doses, which are the actual problem to address first.

meta.subtopic: Prioritising ineffective health self-management in severe hypertension
meta.priority_principle: Address the actual problem driving the risk when there are no signs of acute organ injury
meta.prerequisites: NANDA-I diagnosis structure (actual and risk); signs of hypertensive emergency and stroke
meta.suggested_review: Nursing diagnoses for the client with uncontrolled hypertension

questions.stem: For Rawle's ineffective health self-management, which nursing intervention should the nurse include in the plan of care?

options.label: A
options.text: Repeat the advice to take the tablets daily and give a hypertension leaflet

options.label: B
options.text: Ask the DMO to replace the water tablet with one that does not cause urination

options.label: C
options.text: Refer Rawle to the dietitian for a low-salt diet to bring the pressure down

options.label: D
options.text: Agree a daily tablet routine with Rawle and the daughter that fits market days

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: The priority problem is ineffective health self-management: Rawle takes the tablets only when the pressure is felt and leaves out the hydrochlorothiazide on market days because of trips to the toilet. A routine agreed with Rawle and the daughter, built around market days and with practical support such as a pill organiser, removes the barrier Rawle named and makes daily doses the habit. With no acute organ damage, regular oral doses lower the pressure gradually and safely. Any change in dose timing still needs the DMO's approval.

distractor_rationales.A: Rawle knows the tablets are for the pressure; the problem is when and why they are taken. Advice and a leaflet do not answer the belief that the pressure can be felt or the practical problem on market days, so they are weaker than a routine Rawle helps to design.
distractor_rationales.B: Choosing a drug is the prescriber's decision, and the hydrochlorothiazide has not failed; it has been left off. The urination is an expected effect that better timing can manage, so asking for a new drug moves away from the problem the nurse can act on.
distractor_rationales.C: Less salt helps lower blood pressure and belongs in long-term teaching, but it does not address the priority problem. While the tablets are taken only on symptom days, diet changes alone will not bring 182/110 mm Hg under control.

questions.self_test: Repeating the advice with a leaflet seems reasonable, but information alone does not remove the market-day barrier or the belief behind the missed doses, which a routine Rawle helps design does.

meta.priority_principle: Remove the client's own barriers to daily dosing
meta.prerequisites: Barriers to adherence; collaborative goal setting; diuretic timing
meta.suggested_review: Nursing interventions to support medication adherence

questions.stem: Which action should the nurse perform first?

options.label: A
options.text: Give the amlodipine now and recheck the pressure before discharge

options.label: B
options.text: Hold the amlodipine and clarify the order with the DMO

options.label: C
options.text: Recheck the pressure now and give the tablet if still high

options.label: D
options.text: Give half the amlodipine dose and record the reason

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: At 9:00 am Rawle said one of each pressure tablet was taken with breakfast at 6:30 am, and the stat order makes no allowance for that dose. A second 10 mg of amlodipine today would make 20 mg in one day, twice the usual maximum daily dose of a long-acting drug, in a 71-year-old, risking low blood pressure and falls. The nurse holds the tablet and tells the DMO about the morning dose so the order can be reviewed.

distractor_rationales.A: This follows the written order, but the nurse knows a dose was already taken this morning. Giving it would double the day's amlodipine, and recognising a duplicate dose is part of the nurse's responsibility.
distractor_rationales.C: The pressure is expected to stay high this morning, because the 6:30 am dose has not reached its peak. Making the dose depend on the reading still gives a duplicate dose without the prescriber knowing about it.
distractor_rationales.D: Changing the dose is a prescribing decision, not a nursing one. Half a tablet still adds to the morning dose and leaves the prescriber unaware of the reason.

questions.self_test: Rechecking the pressure first feels careful, but the problem is a dose already taken at 6:30 am, which a reading cannot answer, so the order needs clarifying.

meta.priority_principle: Prevent medication harm, then communicate with the prescriber
meta.prerequisites: Rights of medication administration; amlodipine duration of action
meta.suggested_review: When and how the nurse questions a medication order

questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement in response to the adherence plan?

options.label: A
options.text: No headache reported during the past week

options.label: B
options.text: Potassium of 3.8 mmol/L on the day 5 blood test

options.label: C
options.text: Blood pressure of 144/88 mm Hg with every dose taken

options.label: D
options.text: Passing more urine in the mornings than before

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: The priority problem was ineffective health self-management, and the adherence plan aimed to get both tablets taken every day so the pressure would come down. The empty organiser shows every dose was taken, and the seated pressure has fallen from 182/110 to 144/88 mm Hg. It is not yet at target, but it shows the plan is working and the drugs work when taken.

distractor_rationales.A: Losing the headache is welcome, but it repeats Rawle's belief that the pressure can be felt. Symptoms are a poor guide to blood pressure; the measured reading is the outcome.
distractor_rationales.B: A potassium of 3.8 mmol/L shows that taking the thiazide daily is safe so far. It is a safety check, not evidence that the pressure has come down.
distractor_rationales.D: More urine in the mornings shows the hydrochlorothiazide is now being taken, but it measures taking the drug, not the pressure response the plan was aiming for.

questions.self_test: No headache feels like a good sign, but symptoms do not track blood pressure, so only the measured pressure with doses taken shows the plan is working.

meta.priority_principle: Evaluate the outcome the intervention targeted
meta.suggested_review: Follow-up of hypertension after a treatment change

questions.stem: Which action best demonstrates the nurse's professional development?

options.label: A
options.text: Reflect on the missed cues and set a learning goal on adherence

options.label: B
options.text: Complete an incident report about the earlier clinic notes

options.label: C
options.text: Ask the DMO to do adherence counselling for older clients

options.label: D
options.text: Enrol in a pharmacology update on newer pressure drugs

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: The nurse's own notes from three visits recorded a raised pressure and advice to take the tablets, but nobody asked whether or why doses were missed. Reflecting on what was missed, using a structured model, and setting a learning goal on assessing adherence targets the exact gap this case exposed, which is how a nurse maintains and builds competence.

distractor_rationales.B: No harmful event occurred that an incident report is meant to capture. The issue is an assessment gap in the nurse's own practice, which calls for reflection and learning.
distractor_rationales.C: Adherence assessment is core nursing work. Passing it to the DMO avoids the gap instead of closing it, and the DMO's time is limited.
distractor_rationales.D: Continuing education is part of professional development, but the gap here was asking about missed doses, not knowledge of drugs. A pharmacology update would not change what went wrong.

questions.self_test: A pharmacology update is real professional development, but the gap shown in the notes was assessing adherence, which drug knowledge does not fix.

meta.priority_principle: Target learning at the identified practice gap
meta.prerequisites: Reflective models (for example Gibbs); continuing competence

questions.stem: Which instruction is most important for the nurse to give Rawle?

options.label: A
options.text: Check it whenever you get a headache or feel unwell

options.label: B
options.text: If a reading is high, take an extra tablet and check again

options.label: C
options.text: Check it soon after your morning walk to see your active level

options.label: D
options.text: Check at the same times each day and write down every reading

questions.rationale_correct: CORRECT: Rawle still plans to check the pressure only when it is "felt", the same belief that led to missed doses. Checking at set times every day, whatever Rawle feels, and recording each reading gives a true picture for the four-week review and reinforces that blood pressure is treated every day, not by symptoms.

distractor_rationales.A: This is what Rawle suggested, and it keeps the belief that symptoms show the pressure. Readings taken only when unwell miss the days the pressure is high without symptoms.
distractor_rationales.B: Self-adjusting the dose risks low blood pressure and falls, and it repeats the symptom-driven dosing that caused the problem. Changes to doses come from the prescriber.
distractor_rationales.C: Exercise briefly raises the pressure, so a reading straight after a walk is misleading. Readings should be taken after five minutes of quiet rest.

questions.self_test: Checking when unwell sounds sensible, but it keeps Rawle's belief that the pressure can be felt and misses silent high readings.

meta.priority_principle: Teach to the client's specific misconception
meta.suggested_review: Client teaching for home blood pressure monitoring

pathophysiology:
## Pathophysiology teaching

**Normal regulation.** Blood pressure is cardiac output multiplied by peripheral resistance. Baroreceptors adjust it from moment to moment, and the kidneys, through the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system and sodium and water balance, set it over the long term.

**Chronic hypertension.** Years of raised pressure thicken the walls of small arteries and narrow their lumen, which raises resistance further. The brain protects its blood flow by autoregulation, and in long-standing hypertension that range shifts upwards: the brain becomes used to a high pressure. Diabetes speeds up the same small-vessel damage, so Rawle carries a higher risk to the heart, brain, eyes and kidneys.

**Severe hypertension with and without organ damage.** A reading of 180/110 mm Hg or higher is severe (grade 3 in ESH/ISH terms; the AHA uses 180/120 mm Hg for a hypertensive crisis, and NICE a systolic of 180 or a diastolic of 120). It becomes an emergency when organs are being injured now: encephalopathy (severe headache, confusion, vomiting, seizures), stroke, chest pain or heart failure, retinal haemorrhages or papilloedema, or acute kidney injury. Rawle had a mild headache with an intact neurological examination, a clear fundoscopy, a normal ECG rhythm and no protein in the urine, so the DMO's working diagnosis was severe hypertension without acute organ damage. Because the brain's autoregulation has shifted, a rapid fall in pressure can starve it of blood. That is why, without organ damage, the pressure is lowered gradually with oral tablets over days to weeks (even in a true emergency, specialists aim for a fall of no more than about 25% in the first hour), and why sublingual nifedipine or transfer for intravenous drugs would have been wrong.

**Why it was high: the drugs, taken irregularly.** Amlodipine is a calcium channel blocker that relaxes arterial smooth muscle. It peaks 6 to 12 hours after a dose and has a long half-life, so it reaches a steady effect after about a week of daily doses. Hydrochlorothiazide causes a diuresis within hours, which is why Rawle avoided it before a maxi-taxi ride, and lowers resistance over days to weeks. Taken only when a headache appears, neither drug ever reaches a steady effect (Q2). Hypertension is usually silent, so a symptom-driven routine leaves most days untreated.

**The priority nursing diagnosis.** Ineffective health self-management related to the belief that high pressure can be felt and to the diuretic's effect on market days, as evidenced by doses taken only with symptoms or skipped, and a pressure of 182/110 mm Hg after rest (Q3). It is an actual problem, and it is the cause of the severe reading. An actual problem comes before a risk one unless the risk is more immediately dangerous. Risk for ineffective cerebral tissue perfusion would have come first if there were signs of injury to the brain (confusion, vomiting, visual change, new weakness, a worsening headache); Rawle had none, and without them the pressure must not be lowered quickly, so the risk is reduced by treating the actual problem. The headache (acute pain) is a result of the pressure. Deficient knowledge is one cause within the problem, not the whole of it: no information removes the market-day barrier. Every nursing intervention in the case is aimed at the priority diagnosis.

**Why each decision mattered.**
- Recognising the severe reading instead of accepting the explanation that the clinic causes it (Q1) started the right checks.
- Interpreting the account of pill-taking as symptom-driven dosing (Q2) separated nonadherence from treatment failure.
- Prioritising ineffective health self-management (Q3), once focused questioning found no signs of acute organ damage, put the nurse's effort on the cause of the reading; the DMO's examination then confirmed there was no emergency.
- Agreeing a daily routine with Rawle and the daughter that fits market days (Q4) treated the diagnosis directly by removing the barrier Rawle named, rather than repeating advice or changing a drug that had never been taken daily.
- Holding the stat amlodipine (Q5) prevented a second long-acting dose on the same morning in an older adult at risk of hypotension and falls; regular single daily doses, not extra doses, are what the plan relies on.
- At one week the empty organiser and the fall to 144/88 mm Hg showed the expected outcome for the diagnosis: doses taken daily and the pressure falling (Q6). Sodium and potassium were checked because a thiazide taken daily can lower both.
- Reflecting on three visits of "advised to take medication" (Q7) and teaching scheduled home readings (Q8) address the belief behind the problem.

**Prevention.** Daily dosing whatever the client feels; tailoring dose timing to daily life (a diuretic after the market trip, before mid-afternoon); pill organisers and family support; asking at every visit whether and why doses are missed; home readings at set times; less salt from saltfish, smoked herring, pigtail and stock cubes; weight control, activity and limited alcohol; and regular review of glucose, kidneys and feet.
quality_report: Drafted by Claude (2026-10-10) from CASE_REQUEST NRG-CH-001. Checks run on all eight items. Cover: each stem can be answered before the options are seen (Q1 the severe reading; Q2 symptom-driven dosing; Q3 severe hypertension without organ damage; Q4 daily oral tablets with an early recheck; Q5 hold and clarify a duplicate dose; Q6 the measured pressure with doses taken; Q7 reflection aimed at the gap; Q8 readings at set times). Two-answer: Q1 the callus is a real diabetic-foot concern, but intact skin makes it non-urgent; Q2 'treatment failure' is ruled out because the drugs are not taken daily; Q4 'add a third drug' is ruled out for the same reason; Q6 the headache and the morning urine are deliberate distractors for the belief and for drug-taking rather than response. Cue sufficiency: the 6:30 am dose that Q5 depends on is given in the 9:00 am stage, before the stat order, and is not repeated in the Q5 stage, so Q5 tests recall and integration (hence ASE). Hidden assumption: no standing order is needed; holding and clarifying a duplicate dose is within the registered nurse's scope. The Q5 stage does not mention the morning dose; the plan stage that follows reveals it. Taxonomy: 4 ASE (Q2, Q3, Q5, Q6), 4 AP, no KC. Keys A2 B2 C2 D2. For Jade to confirm: the 180/110 mm Hg severe threshold; whether a DMO in a Trinidad health centre would order a stat dose of the client's usual oral drug in severe hypertension without organ damage; the advice to take hydrochlorothiazide by 2 pm on market days; the A&E return advice; the Chronic Disease Assistance Programme wording; dialect in the client and daughter quotes; and whether a one-week review with sodium and potassium matches local practice. Reviewer (2026-10-10): Clinical and flow review against CASE_REVIEW_BRIEF; no key changed (keys remain C, A, B, D, B, C, A, D). Changes: the DMO's stat order now says 'recheck before the client leaves' instead of 'in one hour', so the case no longer implies an oral amlodipine dose is meant to lower the pressure within the hour, which contradicted Q2C and Q4B (gradual lowering, peak 6-12 h); Q5 option A reworded to match. Q5 rationale now states that a second 10 mg would make 20 mg, twice the usual maximum daily dose, which removes any argument that the DMO intended an extra dose. The plan stage now records that the DMO approves the later hydrochlorothiazide time on market days, so the nurse is not altering administration timing alone (scope). Day 8 bloods are now taken on day 5, since same-morning chemistry is unrealistic for a district health centre lab; the Q6B option and the stage label were updated. The midweek call now comes from the nurse, matching the plan. The opening now states Rawle is a man, matching the population and the daughter's 'Daddy'. Q1 rationale and the teaching section now give the severe threshold as 'at or above 180/110' and note that AHA (180/120) and NICE (180 systolic or 120 diastolic) thresholds differ; the teaching section adds the no-more-than-25% first-hour limit for emergencies. Checked and left as is: Q3 is asked before fundoscopy, ECG and dipstick; Q4 (daily oral tablets, recheck within a week) and Q5 (hold and clarify) differ; Q5's cue (one of each pressure tablet with the 6:30 am breakfast) is on screen from the 9:00 am stage and echoed in Q2 option C, so it is fair recall rather than a hidden fact, and holding and clarifying is within RN scope without a standing order; nurse-performed ECG and dipstick and the one-week nurse recheck are in RN scope. Jade to confirm: which severe threshold the RENR expects (180/110 vs 180/120); that a DMO would order a stat dose of the usual oral drug in this situation; DMO sign-off for the diuretic timing; and day-5 blood timing at the health centre. Revision (2026-10-12): Added home medications to the opening (amlodipine 10 mg, hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg once daily, metformin 500 mg twice daily, no statuses so the 6:30 am dose stays in the 9:00 am narrative for Q5). Charted the stat amlodipine as 'Ordered 10:00 am' on the stat stage (no held/given status before Q5); the cancellation and the DMO-approved new timing are charted on the plan stage, after Q5, and the current regimen again on day 8 without statuses. Baseline examination reordered into body-systems order (CNS renamed Neurological) and Cardiovascular (no ankle oedema), Respiratory (unlaboured), Gastrointestinal and Musculoskeletal normals added. Day 8: pain score 0/10 added; Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Gastrointestinal and Musculoskeletal normals added, including no dizziness on standing. No stem, option or key changed; flow re-checked (Q3 still before the DMO's findings, the Q5 chart shows only the order, Q6 options unaffected). Jade to check: metformin 500 mg twice daily with meals and the market-day hydrochlorothiazide frequency wording on the chart. Revision (nursing focus, 2026-10-12): Q3 rewritten from the medical condition to the priority nursing diagnosis (stem now asks which nursing diagnosis to prioritize; four s.13-form options: A risk for ineffective cerebral tissue perfusion, B ineffective health self-management, C acute pain, D deficient knowledge); key stays B (old B 'Severe hypertension without acute organ damage', new B 'Ineffective health self-management...'); new rationales, self_test and meta.
